meta.cite: Barton O. Oliver's mTOR Atlas. doi:10.5281/zenodo.22059963

data.title: mTOR inactivation governs adaptive survival to ribosome biogenesis deficiency
data.authors: Fan W; Liu H; Yang L; Sinha N; Catipovic M; Dong D; Easawaran H; Green R; Laiho M

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Human cancer cell lines (functional genomics/CRISPR screens)
data.finding: mTORC1 inhibition does not restore ribosome biogenesis but redistributes limited ribosomes away from highly-translated 5'TOP mRNAs toward survival-essential transcripts, defining a 'translational fitness' mechanism that lets cancer cells survive ribosome biogenesis deficiency.
data.abstract_excerpt: Ribosome biogenesis is a resource-consuming process that facilitates rapid growth and feeds uncontrolled, cancerous traits. Constraining ribosome biogenesis and protein translation has become a tenable therapeutic strategy for cancer. Yet, we do not know how cells that rely on high metabolic activity adapt and sustain their growth when deprived of their translational capacity. Conversely, stem cells and treatment-resistant cells persist under low metabolic states challenging their eradication. These are critical questions in cancer therapies.

extracted_findings.intervention: Functional genomics/CRISPR screens under RNA Pol I inhibition; mTOR inactivation (genetic/pharmacologic)
extracted_findings.effect: mTOR inactivation redistributes limited ribosomes from 5'TOP mRNAs to survival-essential transcripts, enabling adaptive survival ('translational fitness') under ribosome biogenesis deficiency
